prompt: The shop buys a one-year Reserved Instance for an `m7i.large` in `sa-east-1`. What has AWS done the moment the purchase completes?
hint: A reservation is a term of payment.

choices.text: Started an `m7i.large` for the shop, which bills from that hour
choices.why: Nothing is started. The shop starts its own instances, and a matching one is then charged at the reserved rate.

choices.text: Agreed to charge a matching instance less
choices.why: Right. It is a discount on the bill, paid for every hour of the term whether an instance matches or not.

choices.text: Set aside a physical machine in a named zone for the shop alone
choices.why: Only a zonal reservation reserves capacity, and even then it is capacity in a zone, not a named machine.

choices.text: Moved the shop's running instances to cheaper hardware
choices.why: The instances do not move or change. Only the rate on the bill does.

prompt: A one-year standard reservation, partial upfront, costs 415 dollars on purchase and 0.04741 dollars an hour. What is its effective hourly rate, to five decimal places?
hint: Spread the 415 over the hours of a year, then add.

prompt: `describe-reserved-instances-offerings --instance-type m7i.large` in the lab answers with `t2.micro` offerings at 0.05 an hour. What may the shop use them for?
hint: Who wrote those prices?

choices.text: As a lower bound on what AWS charges for a reservation
choices.why: They are moto's inventions and bound nothing. AWS's prices come from AWS's list.

choices.text: As the right price for the instance it asked about
choices.why: They are not even about the instance it asked about: the answer named a `t2.micro`.

choices.text: To test code that lists or buys reservations
choices.why: Right. moto keeps a few invented offerings so code has something to call. Every price in the lesson is from the published list.

choices.text: To compare a `t2.micro` reservation with an `m7i.large` one
choices.why: A comparison between an invented price and a real one compares nothing.

prompt: In the table, the EC2 Instance Savings Plan for `m7i` charges 0.09956 and the Compute Savings Plan 0.10915. Which reservations charge those same two rates?
hint: Match narrowness with narrowness.

choices.text: All upfront and no upfront reservations, respectively
choices.why: The all-upfront rates are 0.09292 and 0.10183. The pairing is by class, not by how the money is paid.

choices.text: Standard and convertible, no upfront
choices.why: Right. The narrow plan is priced like the narrow reservation, the flexible plan like the flexible one.

choices.text: Three-year reservations of each class
choices.why: The program prints only one-year terms, and three-year rates are lower still.

choices.text: None: a plan always costs more than any reservation
choices.why: The EC2 Instance plan costs exactly what the standard reservation does, 0.09956.

prompt: A reservation costs 72.68 dollars a month whatever runs; on demand the same machine costs 0.16065 an hour. After how many hours of running in a month is the reservation cheaper? Round to whole hours.
hint: The month's commitment divided by the hourly price.

prompt: A build server runs 220 hours a month. Which costs less for it, and by roughly how much?
hint: 220 × 0.16065, against a flat 72.68.

choices.text: On demand, at 35.34 a month, about half the reservation
choices.why: Right. 220 hours is far below the 452-hour break-even, so the commitment would pay for 510 idle hours.

choices.text: The reservation, because 38% off is cheaper at any number of hours
choices.why: The 38% is off each hour of the term, and the term includes the hours the server is off.

choices.text: The Compute Savings Plan, whose flexibility covers the idle hours
choices.why: Flexibility is about which usage it covers, not about hours with no usage: those are lost.

choices.text: They cost the same, since both are billed for 730 hours
choices.why: On demand is billed only for the hours that ran.

prompt: The shop plans to move its `m7i.large` workload to Lambda within the year. Which commitment keeps paying off after the move?
hint: Which one is a promise about dollars rather than a machine?

choices.text: A convertible reservation, exchanged for a Lambda reservation
choices.why: A convertible reservation exchanges for another EC2 reservation. There is no reservation of Lambda to exchange it for.

choices.text: An EC2 Instance Savings Plan for the `m7i` family
choices.why: It covers one EC2 family in one region. Usage in Lambda is outside it.

choices.text: A Compute Savings Plan, which commits to dollars rather than a type
choices.why: Right. It commits to dollars an hour and covers EC2 in any family and region, Fargate and Lambda.

choices.text: A standard reservation, sold on the Marketplace once the move is done
choices.why: Selling it may recover part of the money, but it pays off nothing after the move; it stops covering anything.

prompt: Which of these are true of a regional standard Reserved Instance for Linux on shared hardware, according to AWS's documentation? Choose all that apply.
hint: Regional is about zones; standard is about exchanges.

choices.text: It covers a matching instance in any zone of the region
choices.why: Right. That is what regional scope means.

choices.text: One for an `m7i.xlarge` covers two `m7i.large`
choices.why: Right. Sizes in a family are counted in units, so the larger reservation covers two of the smaller size.

choices.text: It reserves capacity in every zone of the region
choices.why: Only a zonal reservation reserves capacity, and only in its one zone.

choices.text: It may be sold on the Reserved Instance Marketplace
choices.why: Right. A standard reservation can be sold; a convertible one is exchanged instead.

choices.text: It may be exchanged for a reservation in another family
choices.why: Exchanging across families is what a convertible reservation does, and what its higher rate pays for.

prompt: A Savings Plan bought in `shop-prod` covers 0.10915 an hour. In some hours `shop-prod` runs nothing eligible while `shop-staging` runs an `m7i.large`. What happens in those hours, with default settings?
hint: Lesson 3's consolidated bill, and the order of application.

choices.text: The commitment is wasted, because a plan covers only the account that bought it
choices.why: It covers the buying account first, then floats to the others unless sharing was turned off.

choices.text: It covers staging's instance, as the discount floats
choices.why: Right. In a consolidated bill the discount applies to the buying account first, then to the other accounts.

choices.text: Staging's instance is charged twice, once on demand and once by the plan
choices.why: An hour is covered or not; the negation line exists precisely so it is never counted twice.

choices.text: The plan moves permanently to `shop-staging`
choices.why: The plan stays where it was bought. Its benefit is applied hour by hour wherever matching usage is.

prompt: Put the three lines of one hour covered by a Savings Plan in the order the figure shows them, top to bottom.
hint: The usage, what cancels it, and what was paid.
trap: Putting the fee first is the usual slip: the fee is what was paid, and it only makes sense after the usage it covered has been shown and cancelled.

prompt: Somebody sums every line of type `SavingsPlanCoveredUsage` and `SavingsPlanRecurringFee` for a month and calls it the cost of compute. What went wrong?
hint: Which line cancels the covered usage?

choices.text: Nothing; those two lines are exactly what the plan cost
choices.why: The covered usage is shown at its on-demand value. Without its negation, the hour is counted at its on-demand price and again at its fee.

choices.text: Recurring fees are monthly, so they should be divided by 730
choices.why: The fee lines are already the commitment for the hours they cover; dividing them would undercount.

choices.text: The covered hours were counted twice: the negation was left out
choices.why: Right. Covered usage plus negation is zero; the fee is what was paid. Leave out the negation and each covered hour is paid twice on paper.

choices.text: Tax should have been subtracted from both
choices.why: Tax arrives as lines of its own; it is not inside these.

prompt: For one hour covered by the Compute Savings Plan, the covered usage is 0.16065 and the recurring fee 0.10915. What did the plan save in that hour, in dollars?
hint: What it would have cost, minus what it did.

prompt: A month's bill shows an `RIFee` line for 730 hours and `DiscountedUsage` lines for 490 hours. What do the other 240 hours mean?
hint: The fee is for every reserved hour.

choices.text: 240 hours charged on demand on top of the reservation
choices.why: On-demand hours would be `Usage` lines. These hours had no instance at all to charge.

choices.text: Reserved hours paid for with nothing to cover
choices.why: Right. That is the wasted part of the commitment, and where to look first after buying one.

choices.text: Hours AWS will credit back at the end of the term
choices.why: A reservation is paid for every hour of its term; unused hours are not credited back.

choices.text: A billing error, since the two counts must always match
choices.why: They match only when a matching instance ran every hour. Here it did not, and the bill says so.

prompt: Match each line type to what it records.
hint: Two are negative.

pairs.right: an hour at the on-demand rate
an hour covered by a reservation

prompt: A NAT gateway exists for a whole 730-hour month at 0.093 dollars an hour. What do its hours cost, before any traffic?
hint: Hours times the price.

prompt: Two Elastic IP addresses were kept after their instances were deleted. What does the price list say they cost?
hint: Read the two lines of the AmazonVPC offer.

choices.text: Nothing, because only an address in use is charged
choices.why: The list has an `IdleAddress` line at 0.005 an hour, the same as an address in use.

choices.text: 0.005 an hour each, the same as an address in use
choices.why: Right. 2 × 730 × 0.005 = 7.30 dollars a month, for addresses attached to nothing.

choices.text: Twice the price of an address in use, as a penalty
choices.why: In the list of 17 September 2026 the two lines have the same price.

choices.text: A one-time fee charged when they were released
choices.why: They are charged by the hour while they are held, and releasing them ends the charge.

prompt: The staging NAT gateway passed 200 GB in September. At what monthly traffic would its bytes start to cost more than its hours?
hint: Both prices are 0.093.

choices.text: At 200 GB, where it is now
choices.why: At 200 GB the bytes cost 18.60 and the hours 67.89; the hours are still the larger line.

choices.text: At 1 TB, the first tier of data transfer
choices.why: The NAT line has no tiers. The crossing is where gigabytes equal hours, since the prices are the same.

choices.text: Above 730 GB, the number of hours in the month
choices.why: Right. Both are 0.093, so the bytes pass the hours when the gigabytes pass the hours.

choices.text: Never: hours are always the larger part of a NAT bill
choices.why: A busy gateway passes far more than 730 GB a month, and then the traffic is the larger line.

prompt: Which query finds the four unexpected lines of `shop-staging` fastest?
hint: The usage type names the thing exactly.

choices.text: Cost Explorer grouped by `SERVICE` across the organisation
choices.why: By service, three of the four lines are just 'EC2' or 'VPC', and other accounts' costs are mixed in.

choices.text: Cost Explorer grouped by `USAGE_TYPE`, filtered to that account
choices.why: Right. `SAE1-NatGateway-Hours` and `SAE1-PublicIPv4:IdleAddress` name exactly what to look for.

choices.text: A budget on `shop-staging` with a forecasted alert
choices.why: A budget would have warned that the month was going over. It does not say which lines did it.

choices.text: `aws ec2 describe-instances` in `shop-staging`
choices.why: None of the four lines is an instance, which is the point of the case.

prompt: The shop's database runs all month, every month, and will stay an `m7i.large` in São Paulo for at least a year. Its finance person wants the lowest one-year price and nothing paid upfront. Which row of the table fits?
hint: Nothing upfront narrows it; the machine will not change.

choices.text: Compute Savings Plan, no upfront, at 0.10915
choices.why: It pays 0.00959 an hour for flexibility a machine that will not change does not use.

choices.text: Standard reservation, all upfront, at 0.09292
choices.why: It is the lowest rate, and it is paid upfront, which the request ruled out.

choices.text: Standard reservation, no upfront, at 0.09956
choices.why: Right. The lowest rate with nothing upfront, tied with the m7i EC2 Instance plan; the database runs every hour, far past the break-even.

choices.text: On demand, at 0.16065, since nothing is promised
choices.why: Nothing upfront is not the same as no commitment. A machine running every hour is exactly the case a commitment is for.

prompt: The usage of an hour covered by a Savings Plan is shown at its on-demand cost, and a line of type `SavingsPlan___` cancels it.
hint: The line with the minus sign.

prompt: A Compute Savings Plan of 0.10915 an hour covers the shop's `m7i.large`. For a week the instance is replaced by a larger one whose usage at plan rates is 0.2 an hour. What is charged in those hours?
hint: The plan covers up to its commitment, and no further.

choices.text: 0.2 at plan rates, since the plan follows the workload
choices.why: It follows the workload up to 0.10915 an hour. What is beyond the commitment is not at plan rates.

choices.text: Only the 0.10915; the plan absorbs the difference
choices.why: A plan is not a ceiling on spending. Usage past the commitment is charged on its own.

choices.text: The commitment, plus the rest of the hour on demand
choices.why: Right. The plan covers usage until 0.10915 of it has been charged; the rest of the hour is on demand.

choices.text: Nothing extra, because a larger instance is in the same family
choices.why: Family matters to an EC2 Instance plan's coverage, not to how much a commitment of dollars covers.
